lessons.title: Prediction versus derivation
lessons.summary: Separate your expectation from what follows from the accepted inputs. Predict first, inspect what was supplied, and repair the actual gap.

activities.title: The remark at the desk
activities.objective: Distinguish information in a story from an accepted premise.
activities.explanation: At a fictional repair workshop, Ari belongs to the workshop team. A colleague says Ari has completed the safety check, but that remark has not been entered. The written permission policy requires both membership and the safety lead’s approval. Decide what the workspace can establish now.
tasks: Read the rule and accepted statements.
Predict Ari’s permission before running.
Find the unsupported condition, then admit the provided approval and rerun.
hints: Look for an accepted statement naming both SafetyLead and Ari.
A sentence in this lesson is not an assertion until the workspace admits its formal statement.
activities.solution: Membership alone does not satisfy the two-condition rule. Ari’s permission is initially not derivable. Adding the safety lead’s approval supplies the missing condition. The original FALSE described the inputs, not Ari’s real training history.

setup.text: all $p: member($p, Workshop) & approves(SafetyLead, $p) -> authorized($p, Use, Drill).

question.prompt: Why did the first result differ from what the colleague expected?
choices: The workspace lacked an accepted approval premise.
The engine proved that Ari never trained.
Membership automatically grants every permission.
question.feedback: The formal rule needed an approval premise that the original workspace did not contain.

actions.title: Add the supplied approval
actions.instruction: The fictional safety log now confirms the approval. Add it, then check the same claim.

self_review: Name the missing premise and the evidence that justified adding it.
Explain why the initial FALSE was not a claim about the entire world.

activities.title: Evidence needs a connecting rule
activities.objective: Distinguish a missing rule from a missing fact.
activities.explanation: A separate workshop project contains a review and a team membership record for Bea. The operator expects permission to follow, but has not supplied the policy connecting those records to permission. A reasoner does not invent that connection from familiar words.
tasks: Predict the permission claim.
Identify whether evidence or a rule is missing.
Add the supplied policy and rerun.
hints: Both evidence records are already present.
Search for a rule whose conclusion is authorized; names alone do not define a policy.
activities.solution: The two records do not imply permission without a connecting policy. Admitting the reviewed policy supplies the inference step. Retrieving a document or generating a fluent explanation may help a person find the policy, but neither silently adds it to accepted knowledge.

question.prompt: Which artifact can establish this formal connection in the current project?
choices: Any confident prose answer.
An accepted rule that expresses the policy.
The fact that both names appear in retrieved text.
question.feedback: A derivation uses accepted formal premises and rules; a retrieved passage still needs interpretation and admission.

actions.title: Admit the reviewed policy
actions.instruction: Add the workshop’s supplied requirement rather than guessing a rule from the result you want.

changes.text: all $p: member($p, Workshop) & approves(SafetyLead, $p) -> authorized($p, Use, Drill).

self_review: Separate source retrieval, a proposed explanation and an admitted inference rule.

lessons.title: Precise claims
lessons.summary: Express the intended roles, shared variables, connectives and scope, then test cases that distinguish competing encodings.

activities.title: Who owns the instrument?
activities.objective: Repair reversed argument roles without changing the intended fact.
activities.explanation: A fictional equipment note says Ari owns Meter7. The draft below puts Meter7 in the owner place. It is syntactically valid: a plausible-looking line can still encode the wrong relationship.
tasks: Read the predicate’s named places in the reference.
Predict whether the intended ownership claim follows.
Replace the reversed assertion and inspect the new reading.
hints: The first place of owns is the owner; the second is the owned object.
A valid parse does not compare a statement with the source note.
activities.solution: owns(Meter7, Ari) and owns(Ari, Meter7) describe opposite directions. Replacing the former repairs the encoding. The engine’s compiler can check vocabulary and structure, but source fidelity needs review.

question.prompt: What did successful parsing establish?
choices: The note was accurately formalized.
Ownership is symmetric.
The input used supported syntax and vocabulary, not that its roles matched the note.
question.feedback: Structural validity and faithfulness to the intended relationship are different checks.

actions.title: Correct the two places
actions.instruction: Replace the draft with the intended owner-first statement.

self_review: Identify the source meaning and both argument roles.

activities.title: The unrelated broken item
activities.objective: Repair a rule whose conditions refer to different objects.
activities.explanation: The repair desk invites an owner when that owner’s item is broken. The draft uses $item for ownership and $other for damage. Ari owns Lamp7, while the only damage record concerns Vase2. Test this discriminating case before trusting the draft.
tasks: Predict whether the draft makes Ari ready for a repair visit.
Locate the two variables that should identify the same item.
Repair the rule; then test a genuine broken-owned-item case.
hints: A variable’s spelling controls whether two conditions share a binding.
The damage record can satisfy $other even when it says nothing about $item.
activities.solution: The flawed rule can combine Ari’s ownership with somebody else’s broken object. Sharing $item removes that accidental connection. Adding a real damage record for Lamp7 then supplies the intended positive case.

question.prompt: Why was the unrelated vase a useful test?
choices: It distinguishes shared-item intent from a rule that combines unrelated evidence.
It proves the repair desk policy is complete for every future case.
It makes argument order irrelevant.
question.feedback: A discriminating negative control exposes a rule that a happy example alone would not expose.

actions.title: Use the same item variable
actions.instruction: Replace the permissive rule and rerun the unrelated-damage control.

actions.title: Supply matching damage evidence
actions.instruction: The new inspection concerns Lamp7 itself; check that the repaired rule still admits its intended positive case.

self_review: Explain the wrong binding, not merely the changed character.
Identify both a negative and a positive control.

activities.title: Either, both, and the boundary of a claim
activities.objective: Read conjunction, disjunction and quantifier scope deliberately.
activities.explanation: One inspector has approved Parcel7. First ask whether at least one of two approvals exists, then ask whether both exist. Finally inspect two ownership sentences whose quantifiers occur in a different order. A connective or scope change is a change in meaning, not a cosmetic edit. Run a split-owner inventory that separates those meanings, then repair a free variable that crosses a negative scope using a supported scoped description.
tasks: Predict the OR claim and compare it with AND.
Compile the two scope orders and read their structures.
Explain the difference between one shared owner and a possibly different owner per object.
Use different owners for two computers as a counterexample to the one-owner reading.
Compare a refused cross-scope free variable with a relative condition attached to the selected witness.
Compile the precedence pair, XOR, biconditional, and right-associated implication examples; repair the refused compound negation using the supplied atomic expansion.
hints: OR needs a supported alternative; AND requires both conditions.
A variable introduced inside another quantifier can depend on the outer entity.
Shared free names are factored within one ordinary connected region. Crossing negation, modal, quantified or abstraction boundaries can require an explicit scope and can be refused.
activities.solution: The one-approval setup supports OR but not AND. In the scope comparison, “some person owns every computer” asks for one owner covering the computers; “every computer is owned by some person” permits different owners. Compilation exposes the structure without admitting either sentence. In the supplied two-computer inventory, no single person owns both, so the one-owner query is FALSE; an owner for each computer is TRUE. Reusing a free $p across a negative boundary is refused rather than silently choosing its scope. The repaired description attaches the negative approval condition to its own person witness using it; that same witness fills the owner place. Not every explicit binder shape bypasses the co-reference restriction. Distinct period-terminated statements have independent scopes.

question.prompt: What is the safest way to compare two plausible encodings?
choices: Run only the example both already accept.
Read their structures and run cases where their meanings differ.
Choose the shorter sentence.
question.feedback: A structural reading and a discriminating case reveal different kinds of encoding error.

actions.title: Ask for both approvals
actions.instruction: Run the conjunction on unchanged inputs.

actions.title: Inspect one owner for every computer
actions.instruction: Compile this source; inspect the quantifier nesting without admitting it.

actions.title: Inspect an owner per computer
actions.instruction: Compare the written-order scope using an explicit outer computer variable.

actions.title: Test the one-owner claim
actions.instruction: Admit the supplied inventory and ownership records, then ask whether one person owns every computer.

actions.title: Allow an owner for each computer
actions.instruction: Use the same inventory with the computer quantifier outside the owner requirement.

actions.title: Inspect a free variable across negation
actions.instruction: Compile a draft that repeats an unbound name across a negative boundary. This unsupported scope choice must be diagnosed, not treated as FALSE.

actions.title: Attach the condition to its witness
actions.instruction: Ask whether TerminalA has some person owner without a derived InspectorA approval. The relative it refers to the selected person, keeping the negative condition attached to that witness.

self_review: State the OR/AND difference.
State which scope requires one owner and which allows owner dependence.
Read the formula grouping rather than relying on English precedence, and keep compilation separate from truth and admission.

lessons.title: Evidence
lessons.summary: Follow a conclusion to the assertions and sources it used, review those inputs, and explain what the proof establishes.

activities.title: The wrong cart in the note
activities.objective: Identify and repair a source-to-statement mismatch while preserving the policy.
activities.explanation: Fictional note: “Inspector approved Cart2 for checkout; Cart1 still awaits inspection.” A draft incorrectly asserts approval of Cart1. The policy derives checkout readiness from that approval. Run the draft, then review the input rather than treating the proof as authentication of the note.
tasks: Predict and inspect Cart1’s readiness.
Follow the proof to the approval assertion and read the supplied note.
Withdraw the unsupported assertion, then encode the cart the note actually names.
hints: A derivation can be valid for an incorrectly entered premise.
Compare Cart1 and Cart2 in the exact source sentence.
activities.solution: The first derivation uses the erroneous Cart1 assertion. Withdrawing it makes Cart1’s readiness not derivable. The corrected Cart2 assertion supports Cart2, while preserving the original inspection requirement. Changing the policy to retain the desired Cart1 answer would conceal the source error.

question.prompt: Which check found the error?
choices: The proof automatically authenticated the source.
A TRUE outcome made source review unnecessary.
Comparing the admitted statement with its source.
question.feedback: The proof showed the consequence of the inputs; source comparison exposed the mis-encoding.

actions.title: Withdraw the unsupported assertion
actions.instruction: Remove only the assertion the note does not support.

actions.title: Encode the note faithfully
actions.instruction: The note names Cart2. Assert that approval and inspect its readiness.

self_review: Locate the exact assertion used.
Explain what changed and why the requirement stayed fixed.

activities.title: Three questions about one result
activities.objective: Separate source, encoding and implementation assurance.
activities.explanation: A colleague supplies a clean proof and asks whether it settles the whole engineering decision. Review three independent questions: was the inspection reliable and current; did the formal statement capture the intended observation; and does the implemented reasoner meet its stated contracts? Evidence for one question does not automatically settle the others.
tasks: Run the supplied readiness claim and inspect its actual support.
Identify which concern belongs to the source, the encoding and the implementation.
Write a concrete follow-up check for each concern.
hints: A proof cites a source label; the label does not authenticate the underlying inspection.
Engine regression tests and correspondence arguments address implementation behavior, not the truth of this inspection.
activities.solution: The run establishes a derivation under its inputs and profile. A source review checks the inspection; a formalization review checks the statement; engine tests and scoped assurance arguments check implementation properties. Record the evidence actually available at each boundary instead of calling the whole decision verified.

question.prompt: “The record names Cart3, but the statement names Cart4” is primarily which issue?
choices: An encoding mismatch.
A proof that the inspector lied.
An exhausted search budget.
question.feedback: The discrepancy is visible between source and formal statement; it does not by itself establish a source or engine defect.

self_review: Name evidence still needed at each boundary.
Avoid claiming implementation soundness from a single successful run.

lessons.title: Reasoning outcomes
lessons.summary: Interpret the engine’s four outcomes and their reasons, separately from input errors, refusals, cancellation and your learning check.

activities.title: Missing evidence and an undecided computation
activities.objective: Distinguish a closed-world FALSE from UNKNOWN with a reported reason.
activities.explanation: A project records one approval. Ask about a different reviewer, then inspect a computation that cannot be resolved by the browser’s local arithmetic path. Missing ordinary evidence and unavailable computation cross different boundaries.
tasks: Predict the missing-approval claim.
Run the supplied computation and read its actual UNKNOWN detail.
Choose a next action appropriate to each boundary.
hints: An ordinary unsupported approval is not UNKNOWN under this closed-world profile.
Do not guess why a computation is unresolved: read the returned reason.
activities.solution: The absent approval gives a closed-world FALSE. The nonnumeric arithmetic example requires a path this browser session cannot resolve, so the engine reports UNKNOWN with its actual reason. Supplying the missing approval repairs the first issue; valid numeric inputs repair the local arithmetic example without an external model.

question.prompt: Which statement is accurate?
choices: Every unsupported approval is UNKNOWN.
UNKNOWN needs its reported reason; it is not the name for any missing fact.
UNKNOWN is automatically an operational crash.
question.feedback: Reasoning outcomes and operational failures are different, and missing ordinary support is FALSE in this profile.

actions.title: Supply the missing review
actions.instruction: A new source now supplies the previously absent review.

actions.title: Inspect an unresolved computation
actions.instruction: Run the nonnumeric result term and retain the reported reason.

actions.title: Use a numeric result claim
actions.instruction: Ask whether 5 is the sum of 2 and 3; this can use the local numeric path.

self_review: Name a different recovery for missing evidence and unresolved computation.

activities.title: A decision stopped by its budget
activities.objective: Recover from actual depth exhaustion without turning it into FALSE.
activities.explanation: Use a small classification chain as a controlled search experiment: a dog is an animal, and an animal is alive. The initial depth budget is deliberately small. Compare the recorded boundary with a rerun under a sufficient budget. Then contrast chain depth with a wide quantified dispatch question. Many combinations can exhaust formula work even when no deep inference chain is needed.
tasks: Predict the bounded run’s outcome.
Inspect the reported resource kind and the recorded search.
Raise depth, rerun, and compare the two run settings.
Run the wide dispatch query and inspect its fuel resource kind.
Ask a focused dispatch question without treating it as an answer to the original universal query.
hints: The limit is a property of this run, not a negative fact about the individual.
The old run keeps its original depth and revision after settings change.
The browser has a fixed formula-work allowance as well as configurable chain depth. Increasing depth does not increase that allowance.
A recorded-history limit only limits the displayed history; a proof-construction limit can prevent a complete certificate.
activities.solution: The shallow classification run reports RESOURCE_EXCEEDED with depth as its kind; depth twenty permits that derivation. The wide dispatch query instead reaches the fixed formula-work allowance and reports fuel. Raising chain depth cannot enlarge that allowance. The focused CrewA question is FALSE because its required membership evidence is absent; it answers a narrower question, not the exhausted universal one. The engine allows 1,000,000 formula-node evaluations per verdict search and separately per certificate walk. A 100,000-step certificate ceiling or exhausted certificate walk refuses the whole certificate as a reasoning error. These browser/native limits differ from recording truncation and WASI instruction-fuel or memory controls. No partial certificate becomes a completed Boolean proof.

question.prompt: What did the limited run establish?
choices: Nori is not alive.
Every UNKNOWN can be fixed by more depth.
It reached the configured depth boundary without a completed Boolean conclusion.
question.feedback: Use the returned resource kind; raising depth does not address unrelated admission, encoding or backend failures.

actions.title: Raise the search depth
actions.instruction: Install a depth-20 profile and rerun the same claim.

actions.title: Inspect formula-work exhaustion
actions.instruction: The fictional dispatch policy has eight universal variables. Admit it, then ask the whole quantified question. Read the returned resource kind; no provider or host budget is being simulated.

changes.text: all $a, $b, $c, $d, $e, $f, $g, $h: member($a, CrewA) & member($b, CrewB) & member($c, CrewC) & member($d, CrewD) & member($e, CrewE) & member($f, CrewF) & owns($g, $h) -> ready($a, Dispatch).

operation.claim: all $a, $b, $c, $d, $e, $f, $g, $h: member($a, CrewA) & member($b, CrewB) & member($c, CrewC) & member($d, CrewD) & member($e, CrewE) & member($f, CrewF) & owns($g, $h) -> ready($a, Dispatch).

actions.title: Ask the focused operational question
actions.instruction: If the task is readiness of CrewA, ask that named question. Preserve the exhausted universal run: this focused result does not establish the original universal claim.

self_review: Distinguish a resource outcome from a cancelled or crashed operation.
Distinguish chain depth, formula fuel, certificate refusal, recording truncation and host instruction fuel.
Explain why a narrower question is not a proof of the original universal statement.

activities.title: Compilation is not a verdict
activities.objective: Locate an input error and repair it without calling it FALSE.
activities.explanation: A statement is missing its final period. Compile it and inspect the error. Repairing syntax makes the source interpretable; it does not automatically admit the statement or establish a query result.
tasks: Compile the incomplete source.
Locate and repair the missing delimiter.
Explain the difference between compilation, admission and a reasoning query.
hints: The compiler cannot complete this statement as written.
After the period is supplied, the next result is a compilation artifact, not a truth value.
activities.solution: The first operation fails at the input boundary. The repaired source compiles. Actual admission and querying are separate operations. Cancellation is different again: it records an aborted attempt with no completed reasoning outcome, and may have no captured events after hard termination.

question.prompt: Which item is a reasoning outcome?
choices: FALSE
An input syntax error
A cancelled worker request
question.feedback: FALSE is a decision result. Input errors and cancellation describe different operation boundaries.

actions.title: Repair the source
actions.instruction: Compile the corrected statement without admitting it.

self_review: Explain why a correct diagnosis of an error can complete a learning activity.

lessons.title: Investigating and revising a decision
lessons.summary: Predict, run, inspect, change evidence and repair the release-readiness decision.

activities.title: One approval
activities.objective: Predict whether BuildA is ready with only its automated-check approval.
activities.explanation: A release needs two approvals for the same build. TestRunner has approved BuildA. Read the policy and the evidence before you run the claim.
tasks: Read the policy and the accepted evidence.
Choose a prediction, then run the claim.
Find the condition that has no support.
hints: The policy joins two conditions with AND. Which approval is present? Which one is missing?
Use the accepted inputs and the actual run record; the authored reasoning explains the intended learning check.
activities.solution: TestRunner's approval supports one condition. Reviewer's approval of BuildA has not been asserted or derived. Under this closed-world profile, readiness is not derivable: FALSE. That does not prove the real build unsafe.

activities.title: A different build
activities.objective: Add Reviewer's approval of BuildB, then predict again.
activities.explanation: There will be two approvals, but they concern different builds. The variable $build denotes the same entity everywhere it appears in this policy.
tasks: Add approves(Reviewer, BuildB).
Predict and run BuildA's readiness claim.
Compare the build named by each approval.
hints: An approval of BuildB cannot fill a condition that requires an approval of BuildA.
Use the accepted inputs and the actual run record; the authored reasoning explains the intended learning check.
activities.solution: With $build bound to BuildA, the second condition is approves(Reviewer, BuildA). The new evidence is about BuildB. BuildA's readiness remains not derivable.

activities.title: Same build, both approvals
activities.objective: Add Reviewer's approval of BuildA and inspect what supports the result.
activities.explanation: Give BuildA its review. After running, follow the conclusion to the policy and the assertions used to establish its two conditions.
tasks: Add approves(Reviewer, BuildA).
Predict, then run the claim.
Inspect the supporting assertions and their source labels.
hints: Both conditions now concern BuildA. Inspect the proof to find the actual assertion identifiers.
Use the accepted inputs and the actual run record; the authored reasoning explains the intended learning check.
activities.solution: The checker and reviewer approvals now bind the same build variable. The engine can apply the AND policy and derive readiness from those inputs. A proof establishes that derivation; it does not independently verify the source documents.

activities.title: Replay and proof
activities.objective: Distinguish the operations the engine attempted from the derivation it returned.
activities.explanation: Execution replay includes attempts, intermediate states and failed branches. A proof explains the returned derivation. They answer different questions about the same run.
tasks: Run the current claim if no run is available.
Inspect execution replay and a failed attempt, when present.
Open the proof, then answer the understanding check.
hints: A rejected candidate can appear in execution history without supporting the final derivation.
Use the accepted inputs and the actual run record; the authored reasoning explains the intended learning check.
activities.solution: Replay reads the saved operations and snapshots. It never runs reasoning again. The proof links the steps and assertions relevant to its derivation; it is not a transcript of every operation attempted.

activities.title: Independent support
activities.objective: Add a second review assertion, withdraw one, then withdraw the last.
activities.explanation: Two separately recorded assertions can support the same claim. Removing one assertion need not remove the conclusion if another active assertion still supports it.
tasks: Assert BuildA's review again with a different source label.
Predict and run while both review assertions are active.
Withdraw one review, run, then withdraw the last and run.
hints: Count active assertions, not just distinct statement text. Each withdrawal names one assertion identifier.
Use the accepted inputs and the actual run record; the authored reasoning explains the intended learning check.
activities.solution: Readiness survives the first withdrawal because one review assertion remains. After the last review support is withdrawn, the AND policy lacks its second condition. The engine rebuilds from the surviving assertions. Separate records do not by themselves establish independent real-world evidence.

activities.title: Assert readiness directly
activities.objective: Try to assert the protected conclusion and explain the refusal.
activities.explanation: The readiness relation is declared derived-only. Evidence is admitted through the policy's premises; typing the conclusion directly cannot bypass that policy.
tasks: Attempt to add ready(BuildA, Release).
Inspect the admission refusal and unchanged revision.
Choose the explanation that describes the boundary.
hints: A refusal describes an attempted knowledge change. It is separate from the outcome of a reasoning query.
Use the accepted inputs and the actual run record; the authored reasoning explains the intended learning check.
activities.solution: The engine refuses a direct readiness assertion because that relation is derived-only. No change is committed. Supply the policy's required evidence instead. Understanding this refusal is a successful learning check.

activities.title: Repair a flawed policy
activities.objective: Repair an OR policy so both approvals are required for the same build.
activities.explanation: Work in a separate exercise. The starting rule admits either approval. A single successful example cannot reveal that bug, so test four cases before and after your edit.
tasks: Run all four cases against the flawed policy.
Change OR (|) to AND (&), then rerun.
Explain why the missing-approval and cross-build cases matter.
hints: The checker-only case passes the weak rule. Does 'either condition' express the requirement that both approvals exist?
Use the accepted inputs and the actual run record; the authored reasoning explains the intended learning check.
activities.solution: AND requires both approvals with the same $build binding. The checker-only and reviewer-only cases become FALSE, same-build approvals yield TRUE, and cross-build approvals remain FALSE. The case checks test behavior; compare your written explanation with these criteria yourself.

lessons.title: Comparing neuro-symbolic approaches
lessons.summary: Compare model-only, symbolic and reviewed drafting workflows by their inputs, evidence, failures and maintenance costs.

activities.title: A confident answer is a different artifact
activities.objective: Compare authored model output with an actual symbolic decision.
activities.explanation: Authored illustration, not captured model output: a text assistant says “Two approvals are present, so the release is ready.” One approval names BuildA and the other BuildB. Compare that sentence with the real symbolic run. A reviewed drafting workflow adds a separate opportunity to catch the name mismatch before admission.
tasks: Run the cross-build case.
Compare the authored prose answer with the accepted inputs and proof search.
Identify where a drafting-and-review workflow could preserve or lose the build identity.
hints: The same $build must satisfy both rule conditions.
Review can fail even when the reasoner accurately derives from what was accepted.
activities.solution: The symbolic claim does not follow from cross-build approvals. A model-only response requires its own evidence check; a fluent answer is not a derivation. A hybrid workflow adds reviewed formalization, but an incorrect accepted draft can still produce an unwanted conclusion. The illustration measures no model’s accuracy, speed or cost.
self_review: Name the input and checking method for each approach.
Locate one failure boundary in model drafting, human review and symbolic inference.
Keep authored illustration separate from measured evidence.

activities.title: Who will maintain the knowledge?
activities.objective: Choose an architecture using explicit maintenance and review responsibilities.
activities.explanation: A small operations team wants help deciding whether equipment can be checked out. Policies change monthly and source notes arrive as prose. Compare a checklist, a symbolic policy model and reviewed model-assisted drafting. More automation changes where work occurs; it does not remove responsibility for interpreting policy and updating evidence.
tasks: List who owns the policy, source review, formalization and rule updates.
Choose an initial workflow for this fictional team.
Describe a small trial and the evidence that would make you revise that choice.
Identify which source formats and host capabilities must remain available if the workflow moves to another runtime.
hints: Separate initial authoring cost from the cost of each new note or policy change.
A defensible choice can favor a simpler workflow when maintenance capacity is limited.
activities.solution: There is no universal winning architecture. A useful choice names the errors it targets, the available maintainers, the review load and a way to evaluate behavior after changes. Retrieval can supply source passages; verification can check modeled requirements; neither substitutes for choosing the right requirements. Portability depends on preserving source meaning, supported vocabulary, profile and required host integrations; a portable file alone does not guarantee equivalent execution. This reflection is self-reviewed, not automatically graded.
self_review: Name a concrete maintenance owner and recurring task.
Identify a failure your choice reduces and a failure it leaves.
Specify a realistic trial with counterexamples; do not invent numerical performance claims.

activities.title: Repair an assurance claim
activities.objective: Replace an unconditional promise with a scoped, testable assurance statement.
activities.explanation: A draft proposal says: “The reasoner proves every operational decision correct, so source review and regression tests are unnecessary.” Rewrite this proposal into something the team can evaluate. Consider source quality, encoding, implemented contracts, search limits and decisions outside the model. The research-context reference contrasts an early proposal for formal-premise reasoning with a later modular neural-and-symbolic design. Their publication dates and architectural ideas do not certify this application.
tasks: Identify unsupported promises in the proposal.
Write a revised claim naming assumptions and evidence.
Choose a counterexample or test for each important assumption.
Compare the two research proposals in the reference: identify what is represented explicitly and what the neural modules contribute.
Explain why historical lineage and a research architecture are different evidence from the companion’s tested runtime contracts.
hints: A proof concerns a particular claim, inputs, profile and implementation.
Soundness, completeness, source truth and successful operation under a budget are different claims.
activities.solution: An appropriate assurance statement identifies the modeled decision and the evidence supporting each boundary. Tests can expose defects; a formal argument covers its stated model and correspondence assumptions. Neither a green test suite nor one proof establishes unrestricted correctness. The repaired proposal should retain source review and regression work where they address actual risks. McCarthy’s 1959 proposal centers on manipulating formal statements and drawing conclusions from premises. The 2022 MRKL proposal combines neural models with discrete knowledge and reasoning modules. They illustrate different design choices, not a claim that either paper proves this implementation correct. Use research ideas to frame a design, then evaluate the actual representation, interfaces and evidence for the chosen system.
self_review: State the modeled scope and excluded decisions.
Separate formal-model claims from implementation evidence.
Give an actionable check or repair at each identified boundary.
Identify one architectural connection and one difference between the two proposals without inferring guaranteed accuracy from their dates or labels.

lessons.title: Relationships and scope
lessons.summary: Represent roles, identities, quantifiers, descriptions, modifiers, relatives and modal context with the supported notation.

activities.title: A gift has three roles
activities.objective: Distinguish fixed roles, unspecified places and existential witnesses without silently changing who did what.
activities.explanation: A logistics note records Ari giving Crate7 to Bea. The three places of gives are giver, gift and recipient. An underscore is an explicit unspecified value, not a wildcard that can match Crate7. Omitting a place, including a gap left by named arguments, uses that same unspecified value. Use ? when the intended claim is that some gift fills the place.
tasks: Run the underscore claim and explain why the receipt does not establish it.
Compile the fully filled named-place statement and identify each role.
Inspect the repeated-place error, then compile its syntax repair without treating compilation as evidence.
Decide the named-place omission and compare it with the underscore claim.
Replace the gift placeholder with ? and use Find to inspect the supported gift.
hints: The receipt fills the gift place with Crate7. The unspecified value _ is different from that named item.
Named places route arguments to the existing signature. Leaving gift out still inserts an unspecified value; naming the other places does not turn the gap into an existential.
? introduces a fresh existential witness. Find returns actual bindings for that query; it does not change the accepted receipt.
activities.solution: Both gives(Ari, _, Bea). and gives(giver: Ari, recipient: Bea). are FALSE from this receipt: their unspecified gift does not match Crate7. The fully filled positional and named statements express the recorded roles. Replacing the gift with ? makes an existential claim that is TRUE, and Find returns Crate7 as its gift witness. The repeated giver place is a compile error; repairing its syntax alone does not establish the resulting claim.

actions.title: Read named places
actions.instruction: Compile the same relationship with names instead of relying on positional memory.

operation.source: gives(giver: Ari, gift: Crate7, recipient: Bea).

actions.title: Inspect a repeated place
actions.instruction: Compile the defective draft; locate the place filled twice.

actions.title: Repair the repeated place
actions.instruction: Put Bea in the recipient place and leave gift omitted. This repairs the syntax, but the missing gift becomes an unspecified value; compilation alone does not show that the receipt supports the claim.

actions.title: Check the named omission
actions.instruction: Decide the repaired named-place claim. Compare its missing gift with the original underscore.

actions.title: Require some gift

Its negative queries also expose why closed-world absence is not a classical contraposition certificate.

The negative approval query succeeds by absence even though readiness is TRUE; it does not certify a classical contrapositive argument. Explicit denials and contradiction checks remain separate artifacts.
